guide.title: Chapter C — Hazardous Materials Recognition and Safety
guide.overview: This chapter teaches first responders how to recognize that hazardous materials are involved in an incident, often before anyone says so. It walks through the standard recognition clues: the location, container shapes, markings and colors, placards and labels, shipping papers and safety data sheets, and finally your senses as a last resort. It then covers the main marking systems you will see in the field, from DOT placards and NFPA 704 diamonds to GHS pictograms. It closes with the chapter's core rule: your first operational thought is always safety.
big_picture: Any responder can run into hazmat, and the first call often won't say so: it may come in as a traffic accident, medical aid, fire, or person down.
Recognition leads to safety, and safety leads to lives preserved. If you don't know it's there, you can't protect yourself.
Use the standard clues in order of safety: occupancy and location, container shapes, markings and colors, placards and labels, shipping papers and SDS, and your senses only as a last resort.
Clues are warnings, not absolutes. Placards and papers can be missing, wrong, or unreadable, so cross-check sources.
First operational thought is safety: go slow, keep your distance, and approach upwind, upgrade, and upstream.

sections.heading: Recognizing Hazmat Incidents
sections.simplified:
Any responder can encounter hazardous materials, not just hazmat teams. A federal study cited in the chapter, ATSDR HSEES 2009, found that of the responders injured in hazmat incidents, 58 percent were firefighters, 31 percent were law enforcement, and 11 percent were other responders, including EMS.

The chapter's logic is simple: if you don't know it's there, you can't protect yourself. Recognition leads to safety, and safety leads to lives preserved. The catch is that the first report often won't mention hazardous materials at all. It may come in as a traffic accident, a medical aid call, a fire, a person down, or an investigation.
key_points: Any responder can encounter hazardous materials.
Injuries to responders in hazmat incidents (ATSDR HSEES 2009): 58% firefighters, 31% law enforcement, 11% other responders including EMS.
If you don't know it's there, you can't protect yourself.
Recognition leads to safety; safety leads to lives preserved.
Initial reports may not indicate hazmat: traffic accident, medical aid, fire, person down, investigation.
remember: Firefighters are 58% of responders injured in hazmat incidents; law enforcement 31%; other responders 11%.
Initial reports may not indicate the presence of hazardous materials.

sections.heading: Basic Recognition Clues
sections.simplified:
The chapter lists the standard clues that hazardous materials may be present. Start with the occupancy or location: who is there, and what they make, sell, store, or transport. Then look at container shapes, markings and colors, and placards and labels. Shipping papers and safety data sheets, or SDSs, tell you what is on board, such as the consist on a train. Your senses, meaning sight, hearing, and smell, are a last resort. Other clues include the responsible party, witnesses, and a business plan.

Clues are clues, not absolutes. They are a warning, a note of caution, and an indication of things to come, but not always all the answers you need.
key_points: Occupancy/location: e.g. a plating shop or highway. Hazmat can be anywhere, but know the common locations.
Container shapes: e.g. a compressed gas cylinder.
Markings and colors: e.g. a package label.
Placards and labels: e.g. an orange placard means explosive.
Shipping papers and SDS: e.g. the 'consist' for a railroad incident.
Senses (sight, hearing, smell) are the last resort.
Other clues: responsible party, witnesses, business plan.
remember: Using your senses, especially smell, is a last resort.
Clues are clues, not absolutes: a warning, but not always all the answers you need.

sections.heading: Outward Warning Signs
sections.simplified:
Some warning signs mean something is already wrong. In general settings, watch for people running from or collapsed in the area, and evidence of a leak such as fire, smoke, visible vapors, unusual colors or odors, or a sheen on water. As Michael Callan puts it, clouds are bad, and clouds with color are worse. Other signs include an activated pressure relief valve, recent fumigation like a tented building, dead animals or insects or discolored plants, people with symptoms of exposure, damaged or discolored containers, and anything that just doesn't look right.

At industrial facilities, add alarms from monitoring systems, an activated emergency decontamination shower, a change in paint color on piping, signs warning of unspecified hazards, and unknown liquid in a containment system. The rule: if you see any warning sign, assume hazardous materials are there, and keep looking for clues until you confirm they are absent. The chapter's case studies show how often responders were hurt because they didn't recognize the hazard, such as police chasing a burglar out of a house tented for termites.
key_points: People running from, or collapsed in, the area.
Evidence of a leak: fire, smoke, visible vapors, unusual colors or odors, sheen on water.
"Clouds are bad. Clouds with color are worse." — Michael Callan.
Activated pressure relief valve; recent fumigation (tented building).
Dead animals or insects, discolored vegetation; people reporting exposure symptoms.
Damaged, deteriorated, or discolored containers, valves, piping, or containment.
Industrial signs: monitoring alarms, activated decon shower, pipe paint color change, unknown liquid in containment.
remember: If you see any warning sign, assume hazardous materials are there until you confirm their absence.
Clouds are bad; clouds with color are worse.

sections.heading: Locations and Occupancies
sections.simplified:
Some places obviously hold hazardous materials: a petroleum refinery has flammable liquids, a welding supply business has compressed gases, a garden supply business has pesticides, and an auto parts store has flammable liquids.

Others are less obvious. A swimming pool supply business stores acids and chlorine. A hardware store has flammable liquids. A refrigerated warehouse may use anhydrous ammonia. A soft drink distributor may have compressed or cryogenic gases.
key_points: Obvious: petroleum refinery (flammable liquids), welding supply (compressed gases), garden supply (pesticides), auto parts store (flammable liquids).
Not so obvious: swimming pool supply (acids and chlorine), hardware store (flammable liquids), refrigerated warehouse (anhydrous ammonia), soft drink distributor (compressed and/or cryogenic gases).
remember: Refrigerated warehouse → anhydrous ammonia.
Swimming pool supply → acids and chlorine; soft drink distributor → compressed or cryogenic gases.

sections.heading: Containers: DOT Cargo Tank Trucks
sections.simplified:
A container is shaped the way it is for a reason. The physical properties of the cargo often decide both the shape of the container and what it is made of, so the shape itself is a clue.

The chapter covers five DOT specification tank trucks. The 406, formerly MC 306, has an elliptical cross section and carries liquids, usually gasoline or diesel; it is usually aluminum, which melts in a fire so the tank won't explode. The 407, formerly MC 307, has a horseshoe-shaped cross section from insulation around a round tank and carries liquids with low vapor pressure. The 412, formerly MC 312, is round with external ribs for strength and often carries corrosives. The MC 331 is round with spherical ends, usually steel, and carries compressed gases; the tube trailer is a version of it. The MC 338 is a cylinder covered in insulation and carries cryogenic liquids, meaning liquefied gases.
key_points: Physical properties of the cargo often determine the shape and material of the container.
DOT 406 / MC 306: elliptical; liquids such as gasoline and diesel; usually aluminum (49 CFR 178.346).
DOT 407 / MC 307: horseshoe-shaped from external insulation; low vapor pressure liquids (49 CFR 178.347).
DOT 412 / MC 312: circular with external ribs; often corrosives (49 CFR 178.348).
MC 331: circular with spherical ends, usually steel; compressed gases (49 CFR 178.337).
MC 338: cylindrical and insulated; cryogenic liquids (49 CFR 178.338).
remember: 406 = elliptical, petroleum. 407 = horseshoe. 412 = ribs, corrosives. 331 = compressed gas. 338 = cryogenic.
A 406/306 is aluminum so it melts rather than explodes if the cargo burns.

sections.heading: Containers: Radiological, Tanks, Railcars and Intermodal
sections.simplified:
Radiological packages come in five levels. Excepted packaging survives normal transport and holds very small amounts. Industrial packaging also passes at least the drop and stacking tests for Type A. Type A carries limited, low-level amounts and survives normal handling and minor accidents. Type B is a heavy cask for large, high-activity amounts and must survive severe accidents. Type C is for high-activity material on aircraft and is not allowed for domestic shipments.

Other containers include carboys for liquids, Dewar flasks for cryogenic gases like liquid nitrogen, intermediate bulk containers or totes, marine portable tanks of 110 gallons or more, and compressed gas cylinders. There is no standard color code for cylinders, so you can't rely on color to identify the contents.

For fixed tanks and railcars, look at shape and fittings. Pressure tanks are often bullet-shaped or spherical and painted white or silver to reflect heat. On rail, pressure cars keep their fittings under one protective housing on top, while general service cars often show fittings and may have multiple compartments. Intermodal containers move by more than one mode; IM-101 works up to 100 psi and IM-102 up to 25 psi, while tube modules run 3,000 to 5,000 psi.
key_points: Radiological packaging, least to most protective: Excepted, Industrial, Type A, Type B, Type C.
Type B: survives severe accidents. Type C: aircraft, high activity; not allowed domestically (49 CFR 173, 10 CFR 71).
Compressed gas cylinders have no standard color coding.
Cryogenic tanks: thick insulation; internal pressure can exceed 300 psi.
Low-pressure dome-roof tanks: usually under 15 psi. High-pressure tanks: bullet-shaped or spherical, often white or silver.
Above-ground tanks normally have secondary containment (dikes, curbs, pits) and may be partly covered with earth.
Pressure railcar: fittings in a protective housing on top, not compartmentalized. General service car: fittings often exposed, may have multiple compartments.
Intermodal: IM-101 up to 100 psi, IM-102 up to 25 psi, IMO Type 7 cryogenic, DOT 51/IMO Type 5 at 100–500 psi, tube modules 3,000–5,000 psi.
Intermodal containers are usually 20 or 40 feet long, 8 feet wide, 8.5 feet high; many are 53 feet.
remember: Type B radiological packages must survive severe accidents; Type C is for aircraft only.
You can't rely on cylinder color to identify contents.
Pressure railcars hide fittings under a single protective housing.

sections.heading: DOT Placards and Labels
sections.source_ref: pp. C-18 to C-23, C-37 to C-39
sections.simplified:
The DOT system gives a visible warning that hazmat is present and general information about what type. Placards go on shipping containers like trailers, railcars, and intermodal containers; they are diamonds at least 10.8 inches on each side. Labels go on packages like drums, bags, boxes, and cylinders; they are diamonds at least 3.9 inches on each side. On both, the background color, symbol, and number at the bottom tell you the hazard class. Transport vehicles must be marked with the ID number and placard on each side and each end, and the four-digit ID number can appear on an orange panel or on the placard.

Placards are required for any bulk shipment, for Table 1 materials in any amount, and for Table 2 materials over 1,001 pounds aggregate gross weight loaded at one facility. A mixed load of Table 2 materials may use a single DANGEROUS placard instead, but once 2,205 pounds or more of one category is loaded at one facility, that category's own placard is required too.

Know the nine classes: 1 explosives, 2 gases, 3 flammable liquids, 4 flammable solids, 5 oxidizers and organic peroxides, 6 poisons, 7 radioactive, 8 corrosives, and 9 miscellaneous. Under OSHA, 29 CFR 1910.1201, employers who receive placarded shipments must leave the placards and labels on until the hazard is removed.
key_points: Purpose: a visible warning that hazmat is present, plus general information about the type.
Placards: on vehicles and bulk containers; at least 10.8 inches per side. Labels: on packages; at least 3.9 inches per side.
Background color, symbol, and class number at the bottom identify the hazard class.
Mark each side and each end; ID number on an orange panel or on the placard.
Placards required: bulk shipments, Table 1 in any amount, Table 2 over 1,001 lbs at one facility.
DANGEROUS placard: mixed Table 2 loads; a single category of 2,205 lbs or more still needs its own placard.
Table 1 includes Explosives 1.1–1.3, Poison Gas 2.3, Dangerous When Wet 4.3, Poison Inhalation Hazard, and Radioactive (Yellow III).
Special placards: DANGEROUS, OXYGEN, INHALATION HAZARD (classes 2 and 6).
Other DOT markings: orange panel, stenciled railcars, pipeline markers, FUMIGANT, HOT, MARINE POLLUTANT, orientation arrows, ORM-D.
remember: Placard ≥ 10.8 in per side (vehicles); label ≥ 3.9 in per side (packages).
Table 1 = placard in any amount; Table 2 = placard over 1,001 lbs.
"Placards and labels are a method of communication for you!" — John Falat, CHP.

sections.heading: Special Markings
sections.source_ref: pp. C-24 to C-27, C-40 to C-46
sections.simplified:
NFPA 704 is the diamond you see on fixed facilities. It covers health, flammability, instability, and related hazards from short-term exposure, and it is required by the California Fire Code on industrial, commercial, and institutional facilities. Its colored quadrants are rated 0 to 4. Its limits: it doesn't tell you the quantity, the exact location, or the name of the material.

Other markings you'll see: the biohazard symbol, required by OSHA on regulated waste and on refrigerators and freezers holding blood or other infectious material, with the words BIOHAZARD or BIOHAZARDOUS WASTE; PCB labels required by EPA; and industrial pipe markings under ANSI/ASME A13.1, where color shows the hazard, such as orange for toxic and corrosive fluids and yellow for flammable fluids. Military sites use DOD fire division symbols. Buried pipelines have markers at road and rail crossings stating WARNING, CAUTION, or DANGER, the product, and the operator's phone number, but markers aren't required in dense downtown areas. HMIS is similar to NFPA 704 but meant for employees, not responders. Pesticide labels use the signal words Poison, Danger, Warning, and Caution.
key_points: NFPA 704: diamond with color-coded quadrants rated 0–4; required by the California Fire Code.
NFPA 704 limits: no quantity, no specific location, no material name.
Biohazard labels required by OSHA; signs on entrances list the agent and a responsible person (CCR 5193).
Industrial pipe colors (ANSI/ASME A13.1): red fire quenching, orange toxic and corrosive, yellow flammable, brown combustible, green water, blue compressed air.
Pipeline markers (49 CFR 195.410): at road and rail crossings; not required offshore, at waterways, or in heavily developed urban areas.
HMIS informs employees; NFPA 704 informs responders.
DOD fire divisions 1–6; e.g. Division 1 is mass explosion (octagon), Division 3 is mass fire (inverted triangle).
Pesticide signal words: Poison (pesticides only), Danger, Warning, Caution.
remember: NFPA 704 doesn't identify the material, its quantity, or its location.
HMIS is for employees; NFPA 704 is for responders.
Pipeline markers are not required in heavily developed urban areas.

sections.heading: Global Harmonization System (GHS)
sections.source_ref: pp. C-28 to C-29, C-47 to C-48
sections.simplified:
GHS is the international system for classifying, marking, and communicating the hazards of materials. It communicates through label elements and safety data sheets. A GHS label has a signal word, a hazard statement, precautionary statements, and a pictogram.

There are only two signal words: Danger for more severe hazards and Warning for less severe ones. Hazard statements are standardized phrases tied to a hazard class and category, like "Fatal if swallowed." Pictograms are a symbol inside a red-bordered diamond, such as the exclamation point for irritants and narcotic effects, the flame for flammables, the gas cylinder for gases under pressure, the corrosion symbol, the skull and crossbones for acute toxicity, and the health hazard symbol for carcinogens.
key_points: International system for classifying, marking, and communicating hazards.
Communicates via label elements (signal words, hazard statements, precautionary statements, pictograms) and SDSs.
Signal words: Danger (more severe), Warning (less severe).
Hazard statements are standardized, assigned to a class and category, e.g. "Fatal if swallowed."
Pictograms: health hazard, exclamation point, flammable, gas cylinder, corrosive, explosive, oxidizer, environmental hazard, toxic (skull and crossbones).
remember: GHS has two signal words: Danger (more severe) and Warning (less severe).
Skull and crossbones = acute toxicity; exclamation point = irritant, narcotic effects, harmful.

sections.heading: Shipping Papers and SDSs
sections.simplified:
Shipping papers are the preferred source for identifying hazmat. Each mode has its own name and location. On a truck it's the bill of lading, in the cab near the driver's seat or with the driver. On an aircraft it's the air bill, with the pilot. On a train it's the waybill and consist, with the conductor. On a vessel it's the dangerous cargo manifest, on the bridge.

Shipping papers list the proper shipping name, hazard class or division, UN identification number, packing group, and quantity. Hazmat must stand out if non-hazardous items are listed too. But shipping papers may not always be accurate, complete, or readable, especially after an accident. A safety data sheet, or SDS, is kept in the workplace for each hazardous chemical and gives the chemical name, company, hazards, response information, and chemical and physical properties.
key_points: Shipping papers are the preferred hazmat identification source.
Truck: bill of lading, in cab near driver (49 CFR 177.817).
Air: air bill, with the pilot (49 CFR 175.33).
Rail: waybill and consist, with a crew member/conductor (49 CFR 174.24).
Vessel: dangerous cargo manifest, on or near the bridge (49 CFR 176.30).
Contents: proper shipping name, hazard class, UN number, packing group, quantity.
SDS: required in the workplace for each hazardous chemical used.
remember: Truck = bill of lading; air = air bill; rail = waybill/consist; vessel = dangerous cargo manifest.
Shipping papers may not be accurate, complete, or readable, especially after an accident.

sections.heading: First Operational Thought Is Safety
sections.simplified:
Think safety first, last, and always. A hazmat event is not the time to hurry: a quick response instead of a slow one can kill or injure you and others. Watch out for a negative safety attitude, like "I've been handling this stuff for years" or "Nothing bad has happened to us yet."

Experienced responders use recognized procedures with vigilance and discipline, watch for secondary and tertiary hazards, treat every hazmat event with respect, cross-reference three or more sources before planning, have backup plans for safety equipment failures, and set up decon early. On scene, keep a mental safe approach: keep your distance, approach upwind, upgrade, and upstream, and be a responder, not an indicator.

There are six ways hazardous materials can kill you: toxicity, radioactivity, asphyxiation, explosion, flammability, and corrosion.
key_points: Think safety first, last, and always.
Go slow: a quick hazmat response can kill or injure you and others.
Avoid a negative safety attitude ("I've been handling this stuff for years").
Cross-reference three or more sources before action planning.
Set up and use decon procedures early; have backup plans for failed safety devices.
Mental safe approach: keep your distance; approach upwind, upgrade, and upstream.
Be a "responder," not an "indicator."
remember: First Operational Thought = Safety.
Approach upwind, upgrade, and upstream.
Six ways hazmat can kill: toxicity, radioactivity, asphyxiation, explosion, flammability, corrosion.

The shipping paper for trucks, kept in the cab within the driver's reach.
The shipping paper for aircraft, kept with the pilot.
The shipping paper for vessels, kept on or near the bridge.
A document employers must keep in the workplace for each hazardous chemical, with its name, hazards, response information, and properties.

A diamond at least 3.9 inches per side placed on packages such as drums, bags, boxes, and cylinders.
A rectangular orange panel that can display the four-digit UN identification number.
The most dangerous DOT categories, which must be placarded in any amount.
DOT categories that must be placarded when over 1,001 pounds aggregate gross weight is loaded at one facility.
A placard that may be used for a mixed load of two or more Table 2 categories instead of separate placards.
A secondary hazard a material has besides its main class; it may or may not be shown by a placard.
A container designed to move by more than one mode of transportation, such as truck, rail, and ship.
A rigid container for liquids, often used in labs, holding about 5–15 gallons.
A double-walled, vacuum-insulated bottle for cryogenic gases such as liquid nitrogen.
A stackable, forklift-movable container for fluids and bulk materials; flexible IBCs are called totes.
An intermodal unit of multiple high-pressure cylinders (3,000–5,000 psi) carrying gases like oxygen or hydrogen.
Extremely cold liquefied gases, carried in heavily insulated containers such as the MC 338.
Dikes, curbs, or pits around above-ground tanks to hold a leak.
The color-coded diamond on fixed facilities rating health, flammability, and instability hazards from 0 to 4.
Hazardous Materials Identification System: a color-coded label system similar to NFPA 704 but meant to inform employees.
Global Harmonization System: the international system for classifying and communicating chemical hazards through labels and SDSs.
A single word showing hazard severity: in GHS, Danger (more severe) or Warning (less severe).
A standardized GHS phrase describing the nature of a hazard, such as "Fatal if swallowed."
A GHS hazard symbol inside a red-bordered diamond.
A marking for packages of materials such as consumer commodities that present a limited hazard.
A tank car marked on each side with the proper shipping name of certain materials, such as anhydrous ammonia (49 CFR 172.330).
Keep your distance and approach upwind, upgrade, and upstream.

flashcards.front: Six ways hazmat can kill you?
flashcards.back: Toxicity, radioactivity, asphyxiation, explosion, flammability, corrosion.

flashcards.front: How many sources should you cross-reference before action planning?
flashcards.back: Three or more.

quiz.question: According to ATSDR HSEES 2009, which group accounts for the largest share of responders injured in hazmat incidents?
quiz.explanation: Firefighters were 58%; law enforcement 31%; other responders, including EMS, 11%.

quiz.question: Which recognition clue should be used only as a last resort?
quiz.explanation: Using sight, hearing, and especially smell means you're close enough to be exposed.

quiz.question: A tank truck with an elliptical cross section most likely carries:
quiz.explanation: The DOT 406/MC 306 is elliptical and usually carries petroleum products.

quiz.question: Which cargo tank has external ribs and often carries corrosives?
quiz.explanation: The 412/312 is circular with external ribs for strength.

quiz.question: The MC 338 is designed to carry:
quiz.explanation: The MC 338 is an insulated cylinder for liquefied gases.

quiz.question: What is the minimum size of each side of a DOT placard?
quiz.explanation: Placards are at least 10.8 inches per side; labels at least 3.9 inches.

quiz.question: Table 2 materials require placards when the aggregate gross weight loaded at one facility exceeds:
quiz.explanation: Table 2 requires placards over 1,001 lbs; Table 1 requires them in any amount.

quiz.question: Where are rail shipping papers kept?
quiz.explanation: The waybill and consist are carried by the conductor/crew.

quiz.question: The shipping paper for a vessel is the:
quiz.explanation: It is kept on or near the vessel's bridge.

quiz.question: Which is NOT a limitation of NFPA 704?
quiz.explanation: NFPA 704 does rate health, flammability, and instability.

quiz.question: Which GHS signal word indicates the more severe hazard?
quiz.explanation: GHS uses only Danger (more severe) and Warning (less severe).

quiz.question: The Mental Safe Approach Tactic tells you to approach:
choices: From the direction of the reporting party
quiz.explanation: Part of the Mental Safe Approach Tactic, along with keeping your distance.

quiz.question: Which is NOT one of the six ways hazardous materials can kill you?
quiz.explanation: The six: toxicity, radioactivity, asphyxiation, explosion, flammability, corrosion.

quiz.question: A refrigerated warehouse is a not-so-obvious location for:
quiz.explanation: Ammonia is used as a refrigerant.

quiz.question: Why can't you rely on a compressed gas cylinder's color?
choices: There is no standard color coding
Colors are reserved for the military
quiz.explanation: The chapter stresses there is no standard color code for cylinders.
